transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-30 15:00 PDT · duration 42 minutes · attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Samir (GreenPark Eng Lead), Lena (GreenPark Product), Tom (GreenPark SRE), Jordan (GreenPark Security)

Summary:
- Quick hosted API walkthrough focusing on chat/text gen streaming, parameter tuning, and retry patterns. Demo of Console hints and Redwood Optimize features.
- Customer is evaluating for chat assistant in media CMS with strict latency and content retention considerations.
- Agreed next steps: pricing + security docs + sandbox + follow-up POC scoping.

Topics: Hosted API basics, streaming behavior, params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop), concurrency and rate limits, retries and idempotency, console tips, Optimize recommendations (batching/caching/quantization), security & data residency.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call — im Alex from Redwood, maya's our solutions engineer, we'll walk through a living demo of our hosted chat API and show the console bits that make tuning and cost optimization easier.
[00:18] Samir: hey, Samir here. we've got about 10 million pageviews a month, main ask is a contextual assistant inside our CMS, super focused on latency and keeping costs low.
[00:29] Lena: lena product, looking for safe defaults and easy control over hallucinations.
[00:36] Tom: tom, SRE. curious about connection patterns, streaming vs sync for our web workers, and behavior under retry storms.
[00:44] Jordan: jordan from security — SOC2, SSO, KMS, and data residency questions.
[00:51] Maya: great, thanks. quick qual: current stack? Samir?
[00:56] Samir: we're mostly serverless — node lambdas on GCP, some on-prem infra for compliance docs. hitting about 300 rps during peaks.
[01:10] Maya: ok that helps. for 300 rps we usually recommend a mix: hosted for quick onramp, and Dedicated if you need strict tail-latency SLAs. but hosted can handle pretty high throughput if you tune batching and token limits.
[01:25] Alex: i'll demo the hosted chat endpoint; maya will show console and Optimize suggestions. we'll cover streaming behavior, and then retry/backoff patterns.

--- Demo start ---

[01:37] Maya: opening the Console — here's a saved route for a chat assistant. you can see per-route token rates, tail latency percentiles, and a quick A/B for model variants. i'll start a live request using the playground so you can watch streaming chunks.
[01:55] (audio: brief typing)
[02:10] Maya: sending a prompt: "You are a concise assistant that summarizes an article paragraph-by-paragraph." setting temp 0.2, max_tokens 120, streaming enabled. watch the token stream in the console.
[02:25] (console shows streaming tokens — small delay)
[02:30] Samir: is streaming using server-sent events? how do we reattach if our client disconnects?
[02:38] Maya: good q — streaming uses chunked transfer (SSE-like). if client drops you can resume using conversation state and KV cache, or fetch missing continuation via a subsequent request. we show a sample idempotency key pattern in the SDK examples. note: resuming mid-token isn't safe, so we recommend short-lived reconnect window.
[02:58] Tom: what's the typical latency per token? we care about p99.
[03:05] Maya: depends on model and prompt length; for our curated 2.7B-ish variants you'll see single-digit token latency 10-20ms on NVL100s — but that varies. Console shows p50/p95/p99 by model and sequence length.
[03:23] Lena: you mentioned curated models — is there a fallback if a model is busy?
[03:29] Alex: yes — smart routing policies can fallback to a quantized variant or regional replica. that keeps the app up albeit with slightly different cost/latency characteristics. you can configure automatic fallback thresholds in the route.

[03:45] Maya: switching to parameters: temp, top_p, max_tokens, presence_penalty — tuning these changes creativity vs determinism. for chat assistants we usually start temp 0.0-0.2, top_p 0.8-1.0. increase temp for more exploratory suggestions.
[04:04] (Samir scribbles notes)
[04:10] Maya: important: token budget and truncation strategies. we demonstrated prefix caching — if you include the article body as a cached prefix we avoid re-sending huge context every call, which reduces tokens and costs.
[04:25] Samir: how do we handle long conversation histories without exceeding max context?
[04:30] Maya: two levers: KV cache for key content (summaries, embeddings) and prompt windowing where we summarize older turns into concise notes. Console has a built-in conversation trimming policy template.

[04:48] Alex: ok retry patterns. common pattern: exponential backoff with jitter, idempotency via request_id headers for non-streaming ops. for streaming we recommend short retries only on network blips — avoid re-sending user prompts without dedup because you'll double-charge.
[05:08] Tom: what about partial responses or truncated streams? how do we avoid duplication?
[05:15] Maya: include a client-side state machine: if you see a network error after some tokens, call the status endpoint to confirm whether server completed the generation. if not, reissue with a resume flag and idempotency key. SDKs have helpers.
[05:33] Jordan: from security: is request content logged? where's it stored?
[05:39] Alex: hosted defaults to ephemeral request handling but we have retention controls. enterprise Private/Dedicated options separate control plane and provide customer-managed logging and KMS integration. we'll send SOC2 and encryption notes after.
[05:54] Jordan: and SSO?
[05:56] Maya: SSO via SAML/Okta and RBAC for console. audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM.

[06:08] Lena: can you show a quick cost example?
[06:12] Alex: sure — in Optimize you can see token unit costs by model and an auto-suggest that recommends quantization and batching. for example this route saved 22% by enabling 8-bit quantized variant and prefix caching.
[06:28] Maya: also note continuous batching: for many small chat messages we can micro-batch at the runtime to amortize overhead — console shows batching latency impact and expected token savings.

[06:45] (Demo: run 3 simultaneous requests)
[06:58] Maya: watch how throughput increases and marginal latency steps up — p95 moves from 120ms to 180ms when concurrency hits X because of batching tradeoffs.
[07:12] Samir: what's X?
[07:14] Maya: depends on the pool size and model. console shows recommended concurrency per route based on historical latencies.

[07:25] Alex: ok, quick Q&A about edge cases.
[07:30] Samir: public internet calls are fine but for some docs we need VPC or on-prem, right?
[07:35] Alex: yes — Private deployment supports VPC peering and on-prem air-gapped packages. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity without exposing raw infrastructure details.
[07:46] Tom: do we need any special TLS or mTLS setup for streaming sockets?
[07:51] Maya: TLS for sure; we support mTLS on Dedicated/Private when required. the hosted API is TLS with strong ciphers and per-tenant auth tokens.

[08:04] Lena: a product question — can we tune stop sequences for QA type prompts?
[08:08] Maya: stop sequences are supported; you can provide multiple. be careful with partial token stops — sometimes models include punctuation variations so test with your prompt set. Console has a small A/B harness for stop sequence testing.

[08:25] (20-minute mark summary note appears in console)

[08:30] Alex: we also recommend small integration experiments: first route with low max_tokens and strict temperature 0.0 for deterministic paraphrasing; observe failed generations and tune retries.
[08:45] Samir: sample SDK: do you have node examples for streaming with reconnect logic?
[08:50] Maya: yes i'll paste an example to the workspace. essentially you open a SSE stream, listen for data events, and on error check the "generation status" endpoint. if incomplete, reissue with same request_id and resume flag.

[09:10] (brief pause)
[09:16] Jordan: any mention of PII detection or redaction? we need that in-line.
[09:20] Alex: Redwood has built-in content safety hooks and you can run post-processing in a callback step before storing. for enterprise we provide policy enforcement at route level. we'll send the safety doc.

[09:33] Lena: what about cost control at token level?
[09:36] Maya: per-route quotas, token caps per request, and alerting via Console. you can also set auto-fallback to cheaper quantized variant when cost per token exceeds a threshold.

[09:49] Samir: okay, can you summarize recommended starter config for our use-case?
[09:53] Maya: sure: 1) hosted chat route, model variant = curated mid-size model; temp 0.1, max_tokens 150, top_p 0.95; 2) enable prefix caching for article bodies; 3) set p99 latency SLO alerting in console; 4) retry policy: exponential backoff with jitter, idempotency keys for non-stream ops, resume logic for short disconnects; 5) set quota alert at 80% estimated monthly spend.

[10:25] Alex: wrap-up — we'll send a sample prompt set and a sandbox invite. any final Qs?
[10:31] Tom: last one — can we run a soak test to validate p99 at 300 rps?
[10:36] Maya: yes; for hosted we'll run a benchmark in our sandbox account and share the results; if you need sustained 300 rps p99 < 250ms we might recommend Dedicated.

[10:50] (meeting moves to closing logistics)

[11:00] Alex: action items recap: i'll send pricing and hosted vs dedicated comparison; maya sends SDK snippets and security pack; samir to share user flows. we'll tentatively meet 2026-09-07 for POC scoping.
[11:18] Lena: thanks, this was helpful.
[11:20] Samir: thanks.

(transcription notes: occasional word swaps: "KV cache" transcribed sometimes as "K V cache"; "quantized" sometimes appears as "count-ized"; speaker attribution occasionally generic.)

End of transcript.
